overview: Python provides scalar data types (int, float, complex, bool, str) and four core built-in collection types (list, tuple, set, dict) that cover the vast majority of data-handling needs.

These collections differ along three key axes that interviewers probe: mutability (can it change after creation), ordering (does it preserve insertion order), and whether elements/keys must be unique and hashable.
Comprehensions provide a concise, fast, and readable way to build lists, sets, and dicts, making them central to idiomatic Python data engineering code.
learningObjectives: Identify the core scalar types (int, float, bool, str) and the four collections (list, tuple, set, dict), and explain their mutability and ordering.
Choose the right collection for a task based on mutability, ordering, uniqueness, and lookup performance.
Write list, set, and dict comprehensions and perform common operations on each collection efficiently.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Python's built-in data types include immutable scalars (int, float, bool, str) and four container types: list (a mutable, ordered sequence), tuple (an immutable, ordered sequence), set (a mutable, unordered collection of unique hashable elements), and dict (a mutable, insertion-ordered mapping of unique hashable keys to values). Sets and dict keys rely on hashing for average O(1) membership and lookup.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of the collections as different containers. A list is like a shopping list you can reorder and edit. A tuple is like a sealed record (a coordinate pair) you cannot change. A set is like a bag of unique stickers with no duplicates and no fixed order. A dict is like a labeled filing cabinet where each label (key) points to a folder (value).
coreConcept.historicalContext: Lists, tuples, sets, and dicts have been core to Python since its early versions. A major change came in Python 3.7 (2017), when dictionaries officially became guaranteed to preserve insertion order (an implementation detail since CPython 3.6). Comprehensions evolved from list comprehensions (Python 2.0, 2000) to dict and set comprehensions (Python 2.7/3.0).

whyItMatters.business: Choosing the right data structure determines whether data jobs run in seconds or hours and whether results are correct, directly affecting cost and the reliability of analytics that drive decisions.
whyItMatters.engineering: Collections are the building blocks of every pipeline; understanding their performance (O(1) dict/set lookups vs O(n) list scans) and mutability prevents bugs and slow code.
whyItMatters.scalability: Using sets/dicts for membership and deduplication instead of lists turns quadratic algorithms into linear ones, which is the difference between scalable and unscalable pipelines.
whyItMatters.cost: Efficient structures reduce CPU and memory consumption; immutable tuples and frozensets can be cheaper to hash and safer to share across tasks.
whyItMatters.reliability: Immutability (tuples) prevents accidental mutation bugs, and using dicts/sets correctly avoids subtle errors like unhashable keys or duplicate data.

coreComponents.name: Scalar Types (int, float, bool, str)
coreComponents.definition: Immutable single-value types: arbitrary-precision integers, double-precision floats, booleans (a subclass of int), and Unicode text strings.
coreComponents.purpose: To represent numbers, true/false flags, and text, the atomic values stored inside collections.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Holding individual values, supporting arithmetic/comparison/string operations, and being immutable and hashable so they can serve as dict keys or set members.

coreComponents.name: Sequences (list and tuple)
coreComponents.definition: Ordered collections indexed by position: list is mutable and tuple is immutable.
coreComponents.purpose: To store ordered data; lists for collections that change, tuples for fixed records and dict keys.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Preserving order, supporting indexing/slicing/iteration; lists support append/insert/remove, tuples are fixed and hashable.

coreComponents.name: set and dict (Hash-based collections)
coreComponents.definition: set is a mutable, unordered collection of unique hashable elements; dict is a mutable, insertion-ordered mapping of unique hashable keys to values.
coreComponents.purpose: set for membership tests and deduplication; dict for key-based lookups and associative data.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Providing average O(1) membership/lookup via hashing, enforcing element/key uniqueness, and requiring hashable elements/keys.

internalWorking: Lists are implemented as dynamic arrays of object references, giving O(1) indexing and amortized O(1) append, but O(n) insertion/removal at the front and O(n) membership tests.
Sets and dicts use hash tables: each element/key is hashed to find its slot, giving average O(1) membership and lookup, which is why elements/keys must be hashable (immutable) types.
Tuples are fixed-size immutable sequences; because they cannot change, they are hashable (if their contents are) and can be used as dict keys or set members, unlike lists.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Raw values (int/float/bool/str) -> stored in containers -> list (ordered, mutable) | tuple (ordered, immutable) | set (unique, hashed) | dict (key->value, hashed) -> chosen by mutability/ordering/uniqueness/lookup needs
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An engineer reads raw event IDs into a list to preserve their order of arrival.
2. To deduplicate, the list is converted to a set, dropping repeats in average O(1) per element.
3. Lookup metadata per ID is stored in a dict for O(1) access by key.
4. Immutable (latitude, longitude) tuples are used as composite dict keys because tuples are hashable while lists are not.

keyTerminology.meaning: Whether an object can be changed after creation; list/set/dict are mutable, while tuple/str/int are immutable.
keyTerminology.importance: Immutable objects are hashable and safe to share; mutability enables in-place updates but can cause aliasing bugs.

keyTerminology.meaning: An object with a stable hash value over its lifetime, required for set elements and dict keys; immutable built-ins are hashable.
keyTerminology.importance: Explains why lists and dicts cannot be set elements or dict keys, but tuples (of hashable items) and strings can.

keyTerminology.meaning: A concise expression to build a list, set, or dict from an iterable, optionally with filtering, e.g., [x*2 for x in xs if x > 0].
keyTerminology.importance: More readable and often faster than equivalent loops; a core idiom and frequent interview topic.

importantConcepts.explanation: Use a list for ordered, changeable sequences; a tuple for fixed records, multiple return values, and hashable composite keys; a set for uniqueness and fast membership tests/deduplication; a dict for key-based lookups and associative mappings. Membership in a set/dict is O(1) vs O(n) in a list.
Lists and tuples are ordered by position. Dicts preserve insertion order (guaranteed since Python 3.7). Sets are unordered; you must not rely on any iteration order from a set.

variationsAndTypes: **Numeric:** int (arbitrary precision), float (double precision), complex; bool is a subclass of int.
**Immutable variants:** tuple (immutable list), frozenset (immutable, hashable set), str/bytes (immutable text/binary).
**Comprehension forms:** list comprehension [..], set comprehension {..}, dict comprehension {k: v ..}, and generator expressions (..).
advantages: **Right Tool per Job:** Four distinct collections cover ordered, immutable, unique, and key-value needs.
**Fast Lookups:** set/dict give average O(1) membership and key access.
**Safety via Immutability:** Tuples and frozensets prevent accidental mutation and can be hashed.
**Concise Construction:** Comprehensions build collections readably and efficiently.
disadvantages: **Misuse Costs Performance:** Using a list for membership tests yields O(n) scans instead of O(1).
**Hashability Constraints:** Sets/dict keys require hashable (immutable) elements, so lists/dicts cannot be keys.
**Set Unordered:** Sets give no order guarantee, surprising those expecting insertion order.
**Mutation Aliasing:** Shared mutable lists/dicts can be changed unexpectedly through aliases.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use list for ordered mutable data, tuple for fixed/hashable records, set for uniqueness and membership, and dict for associative lookups; reach for comprehensions to build them cleanly.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid lists for frequent membership tests (use a set), avoid sets when order matters, and avoid mutable types as dict keys or set elements (use tuples/frozensets).

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Imagine organizing a warehouse. A list is a numbered conveyor belt (ordered, items can be added/removed). A tuple is a sealed shipping crate (fixed contents). A set is a bin of unique part numbers (no duplicates, no particular order). A dict is a shelf of labeled bins where each label instantly leads you to its contents.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Tuples are just immutable lists with no other purpose.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Because tuples are immutable and hashable, they can be dict keys and set elements, used for fixed records and multiple return values, which lists cannot do, and they signal that data should not change.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Sets and dicts have no order, so neither preserves insertion order.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Dicts preserve insertion order (guaranteed since Python 3.7), while sets do not. They are different: rely on dict ordering, but never on set ordering.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Replace O(n) list membership with O(1) set/dict lookups to keep pipelines linear; deduplicate with sets rather than nested loops.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Prefer tuples/frozensets for data that must not change to avoid aliasing/mutation bugs across pipeline stages.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Immutable structures are safe to share across retries and tasks; defensive copying of mutable collections prevents one task from corrupting another's data.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track memory usage: large lists/dicts can dominate memory; sets/dicts have higher per-element overhead than lists due to hash tables.
productionConsiderations.security: Be cautious deserializing untrusted data into collections; validate keys/values and avoid using untrusted input directly as dict keys in security-sensitive logic.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Choosing the correct structure reduces CPU/memory; generator expressions stream data instead of materializing huge lists, cutting memory cost.
productionConsiderations.performance: Know the complexity: list index/append O(1), list membership O(n); set/dict membership and dict key access average O(1); use comprehensions and built-ins over manual loops.

codeExamples.title: Contrasting list, tuple, set, and dict
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates mutability, ordering, uniqueness, and lookup across the four core collections in a data context.
codeExamples.code:
# list: ordered, mutable, allows duplicates
event_ids = [101, 102, 102, 103]
event_ids.append(104)        # mutable
print(event_ids[0])           # ordered -> 101

# tuple: ordered, immutable, hashable
coord = (40.71, -74.00)
# coord[0] = 0  # would raise TypeError (immutable)
locations = {coord: "NYC"}    # tuple used as a dict key

# set: unordered, unique, fast membership
unique_ids = set(event_ids)   # drops duplicate 102
print(102 in unique_ids)      # O(1) membership -> True

# dict: insertion-ordered key->value, O(1) lookup
status = {101: "ok", 102: "retry"}
status[103] = "ok"            # mutable
print(status[102])            # O(1) lookup -> retry
print(list(status.keys()))    # insertion order preserved
codeExamples.breakdown: The list keeps order and duplicates and is mutable. The tuple is immutable and hashable, so it works as a dict key. The set deduplicates and gives O(1) membership. The dict maps keys to values with O(1) lookup and preserves insertion order (Python 3.7+).
codeExamples.commonIssues: Trying to mutate a tuple raises TypeError; using a list as a dict key/set element raises TypeError (unhashable); relying on set ordering is unsafe.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use a set for membership tests instead of `x in some_list` to go from O(n) to O(1); use a tuple key for composite lookups.

codeExamples.title: Comprehensions for list, set, and dict
codeExamples.overview: Builds collections concisely with comprehensions, including filtering, a core idiom in data transformation.
codeExamples.breakdown: The list comprehension filters with a condition. The set comprehension collects unique keys. The aggregation uses dict.get with a default to accumulate totals, and the dict comprehension inverts a mapping. These idioms replace verbose manual loops.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Inverting a dict loses data if values are not unique; comprehensions that are too dense hurt readability; forgetting `.items()` when iterating key-value pairs.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use collections.defaultdict(int) or Counter for aggregation; use generator expressions ( .. ) instead of list comprehensions when you only iterate once to save memory.

codeExamples.title: Performance: set vs list membership and deduplication
codeExamples.overview: Shows why sets dramatically outperform lists for membership and dedup at scale, a key data engineering decision.
codeExamples.code:
import time

big = list(range(1_000_000))
big_set = set(big)
target = 999_999

# O(n) membership in a list
start = time.perf_counter()
result_list = target in big          # scans up to 1M items
list_time = time.perf_counter() - start

# O(1) average membership in a set
start = time.perf_counter()
result_set = target in big_set       # single hash lookup
set_time = time.perf_counter() - start

print(f"list membership: {list_time:.6f}s")
print(f"set membership : {set_time:.6f}s")

# Deduplicate in one step
with_dupes = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3]
print(list(set(with_dupes)))         # unique values (order not guaranteed)
codeExamples.breakdown: Membership in a list scans elements (O(n)), while membership in a set is a single average O(1) hash lookup. The example also deduplicates a list by converting to a set. The set lookup is typically orders of magnitude faster on large inputs.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
list membership: <larger>s
set membership : <much smaller>s
[1, 2, 3]  (order may vary)
codeExamples.commonIssues: Converting to a set loses order and duplicates; the exact timings vary by machine; set construction itself costs O(n), so it pays off when you do many lookups.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Build a set once and reuse it for repeated membership tests; to deduplicate while preserving order, use dict.fromkeys(seq) since dicts keep insertion order.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A data team ingests a daily stream of user events and must deduplicate event IDs, count events per user, and attach metadata, then output a clean summary, choosing collections that keep the job fast and correct.
endToEndExample.inputData: A list of event tuples (event_id, user_id, amount), containing duplicates and zero-amount events.
endToEndExample.architecture: An in-memory Python transform that uses a set for deduplication, a dict (or Counter) for per-user counts, tuples for immutable composite keys, and comprehensions to shape the output.
processingSteps: 1. Load raw events into a list to preserve arrival order.
2. Deduplicate event IDs by tracking a set of seen IDs.
3. Count events per user with a dict using .get defaults (or collections.Counter).
4. Use (user_id, date) tuples as composite dict keys for daily aggregates.
5. Build the final summary with a dict comprehension and emit it.
endToEndExample.output: A dictionary mapping each user to their deduplicated event count and total amount, with insertion order preserved for deterministic output.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Log counts before and after deduplication and track memory of the set/dict to detect cardinality spikes.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Skip and log malformed tuples; ensure keys are hashable (use tuples, not lists); handle zero amounts explicitly rather than via truthiness.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A correct, fast summary that demonstrates choosing the right collection per task: set for uniqueness, dict for associative aggregation, tuple for hashable composite keys, and list for ordered ingestion.

industryUseCases.problem: Removing duplicate records (e.g., repeated event IDs) from large ingested datasets efficiently.
industryUseCases.solution: Track seen identifiers in a set for average O(1) membership, or use dict.fromkeys to dedupe while preserving order.
industryUseCases.benefits: Turns an O(n^2) nested-loop dedup into a linear pass, drastically cutting runtime on large data.

industryUseCases.problem: Counting and summing metrics grouped by key (e.g., revenue per customer).
industryUseCases.solution: Use dicts (or collections.Counter/defaultdict) keyed by the grouping field for O(1) updates and lookups.
industryUseCases.benefits: Concise, fast grouping without external dependencies, with insertion-ordered, deterministic output.

industryUseCases.problem: Indexing data by composite keys such as (latitude, longitude) or (user_id, date).
industryUseCases.solution: Use immutable, hashable tuples as dict keys to map composite keys to values.
industryUseCases.benefits: Enables O(1) lookups on multi-field keys safely, which lists cannot do because they are unhashable.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Use sets/dicts (O(1)) instead of lists (O(n)) for membership and grouping so pipelines scale linearly; stream with generator expressions to avoid materializing huge lists.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Immutable tuples/frozensets are safe to share across retries and parallel tasks; defensively copy mutable collections passed between stages to avoid cross-task corruption.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Data-structure choice is local to compute, but efficient structures reduce job time and resource contention, indirectly improving the availability of shared clusters.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Deterministic, insertion-ordered dict output makes results reproducible, simplifying reruns and validation after recovery.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Pick structures by complexity: list append/index O(1) but membership O(n); set/dict membership and dict access average O(1). Prefer comprehensions and built-ins, and Counter/defaultdict for aggregation.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Generator expressions and right-sized structures cut memory; remember sets/dicts carry hash-table overhead, so very large key sets consume more memory than equivalent lists.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Validate external data before using it as dict keys/set members; avoid deserializing untrusted input into collections without checks, and guard against hash-collision DoS in untrusted-key scenarios.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track cardinality (set/dict sizes) and memory footprint; sudden growth can indicate data quality issues like exploding key spaces.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Use sets to detect duplicates and dict keys to enforce uniqueness; validate that keys are hashable and values conform to expected types.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log pre/post-dedup counts and per-key cardinalities; alert when unique key counts or collection sizes exceed expected bounds.

recommendedPractices: **Choose by Need:** list for ordered/mutable, tuple for fixed/hashable, set for unique/membership, dict for key-value lookups.
**Use Sets for Membership/Dedup:** Replace O(n) list scans with O(1) set lookups.
**Prefer Comprehensions:** Build collections concisely and efficiently with comprehensions and generator expressions.
**Use Tuples/frozensets as Keys:** For composite or hashable keys, since lists/dicts are unhashable.
engineeringStandards: Default to immutable types (tuple/frozenset) for data that should not change.
Use collections.Counter/defaultdict for counting and grouping instead of manual dict bookkeeping where it improves clarity.
Never rely on set iteration order; rely on dict insertion order only when documented as needed.
designRecommendations: Build a set/dict once and reuse it for repeated lookups rather than rebuilding.
Use dict.fromkeys(seq) to deduplicate while preserving order.
Stream large data with generator expressions instead of materializing giant lists.
namingConventions: Name collections by their content and structure, e.g., seen_ids (set), user_totals (dict), event_rows (list).
Pluralize collection names to signal multiplicity, e.g., prices, records.
documentationStandards: Document the chosen collection and why (e.g., 'set for O(1) dedup').
Note any reliance on dict insertion ordering and the minimum Python version (3.7+).
Document key structure for dicts with composite tuple keys.
testingStrategies: Test deduplication and grouping logic with inputs containing duplicates, zeros, and empties.
Assert membership performance assumptions by using sets where lookups are frequent.
Test that composite keys (tuples) behave correctly and remain hashable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a list for frequent membership tests.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Lists are the default collection many reach for, and `x in my_list` looks innocent.
commonMistakes.impact: Membership is O(n), so repeated checks over large lists create O(n^2) behavior and slow pipelines dramatically.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Convert to a set once and test membership with O(1) average lookups, or use a dict if you also need associated values.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to use a list or dict as a dict key or set element.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers want composite keys but reach for a mutable collection.
commonMistakes.impact: Raises TypeError: unhashable type, because keys/elements must be hashable (immutable).
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use an immutable tuple (or frozenset) as the key, since tuples of hashable items are hashable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Relying on set iteration order or assuming dict order in old Python.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Confusion between set (unordered) and dict (insertion-ordered since 3.7).
commonMistakes.impact: Non-deterministic output from sets and incorrect assumptions on pre-3.7 dicts cause flaky, hard-to-reproduce bugs.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Never depend on set order; sort explicitly when order matters. Rely on dict insertion order only on Python 3.7+.

comparisonSection.explanation: Lists are mutable and best for ordered collections that change over time; they cannot be dict keys. Tuples are immutable and hashable, ideal for fixed records, multiple return values, and composite dict keys, and they signal that data should not change.

Sets store unique, hashable elements and give average O(1) membership tests and easy deduplication, but are unordered. Lists allow duplicates and preserve order but have O(n) membership. Use a set for fast lookups/dedup and a list when order or duplicates matter.

comparisonSection.optionB: list (position -> value, O(1) index but O(n) search)
comparisonSection.explanation: Dicts map hashable keys to values with average O(1) key lookup and insertion-ordered iteration (3.7+), perfect for associative data. Lists index by position in O(1) but searching by value is O(n). Choose a dict for key-based access and a list for ordered sequences.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the four core collection types in Python and how do they differ?
beginnerQuestions.answer: list (ordered, mutable, allows duplicates), tuple (ordered, immutable, hashable), set (unordered, unique elements, O(1) membership), and dict (insertion-ordered mapping of unique hashable keys to values with O(1) lookup).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Anchor the answer on mutability, ordering, uniqueness, and lookup performance, the four axes interviewers care about.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A list is mutable (you can add, remove, or change elements) and not hashable, while a tuple is immutable and hashable, so tuples can be used as dict keys or set elements and are used for fixed records and multiple return values.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Mention immutability implies hashability and the typical use cases for each.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why are dict key lookups and set membership O(1) while list membership is O(n)?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Dicts and sets are backed by hash tables: an element/key is hashed to locate its slot directly, giving average O(1) access. A list is a contiguous array, so searching for a value requires scanning elements until found, which is O(n).
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This is why frequent membership tests should use sets/dicts and why keys/elements must be hashable.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you deduplicate a list, and how do you do it while preserving order?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Convert to a set with set(my_list) to drop duplicates (order not preserved). To preserve order, use list(dict.fromkeys(my_list)), which relies on dict insertion ordering (Python 3.7+).
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show awareness that sets lose order while dict.fromkeys keeps it.

advancedQuestions.question: Why can a tuple be a dict key but a list cannot, and what about a tuple containing a list?
advancedQuestions.answer: Dict keys must be hashable. Tuples are immutable and hashable if all their elements are hashable, so they can be keys. Lists are mutable and therefore unhashable. A tuple that contains a list is not hashable, so it also cannot be a key.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding that hashability propagates: an immutable container of mutable items is still unhashable.

advancedQuestions.question: Compare list comprehensions, generator expressions, and explicit loops for building collections at scale.
advancedQuestions.answer: List comprehensions build the entire list in memory and are concise and fast. Generator expressions produce items lazily, using minimal memory, ideal when you iterate once over large data. Explicit loops are most flexible but verbose and usually slower than comprehensions.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Mention memory trade-offs: prefer generators for large, single-pass streams to avoid materializing huge lists.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A pipeline checks whether each of 10 million incoming IDs has been seen before, using `if id in seen_list`. It is extremely slow. How do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Recognize that list membership is O(n), making the overall check O(n^2). The fix is a hash-based structure for O(1) membership, then confirm uniqueness semantics.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Replace the list with a set: maintain `seen = set()` and use `if id in seen` for O(1) average membership, adding new IDs with `seen.add(id)`. This reduces the overall complexity from O(n^2) to O(n).

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an in-memory deduplication and per-key aggregation component for a streaming ingestion job in Python.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Maintain a set of seen IDs for O(1) dedup, a dict (or collections.Counter/defaultdict) keyed by the grouping field for counts/sums, and use immutable tuples as composite keys where multi-field grouping is needed; emit results from an insertion-ordered dict.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Sets/dicts give fast lookups but consume more memory due to hash tables; if memory is constrained at very high cardinality, consider probabilistic structures (e.g., Bloom filters) at the cost of exact accuracy.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: For volumes exceeding single-node memory, partition by key (e.g., hash of user_id) and process shards independently, or offload aggregation to a distributed engine, keeping the same set/dict patterns per partition.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Python's core collections are list (ordered, mutable), tuple (ordered, immutable, hashable), set (unique, unordered, O(1) membership), and dict (insertion-ordered key->value, O(1) lookup).
keyConcepts: list: ordered, mutable, duplicates allowed, O(n) membership.
tuple: ordered, immutable, hashable (usable as dict key/set element).
set: unordered, unique hashable elements, average O(1) membership/dedup.
dict: insertion-ordered (3.7+) mapping of unique hashable keys -> values, O(1) lookup.
Comprehensions: [x for x in xs], {x for x in xs}, {k: v for ..} build collections concisely.
formulas: set/dict membership and dict key lookup: average O(1)
commands: s = set(lst); 2 in s                   # O(1) membership / dedup
d = {"a": 1}; d.get("b", 0)          # dict lookup with default
{k: v for k, v in pairs}               # dict comprehension
interviewPoints: Know mutability/ordering/uniqueness for all four collections.
set/dict membership is O(1); list membership is O(n).
Only hashable (immutable) objects can be dict keys / set elements.
Dicts preserve insertion order since Python 3.7; sets do not.
Use comprehensions/generators; dedupe with set or dict.fromkeys (order-preserving).
quickNotes: bool is a subclass of int; True == 1 and False == 0.
Tuples enable multiple return values and composite dict keys.
frozenset is the immutable, hashable version of set.
Use collections.Counter/defaultdict for counting and grouping.
Generator expressions (..) stream data, saving memory vs list comprehensions.

keyTakeaways: Python's four core collections differ by mutability, ordering, uniqueness, and lookup: list (ordered, mutable), tuple (ordered, immutable, hashable), set (unique, unordered), dict (insertion-ordered key->value).
Sets and dicts use hash tables for average O(1) membership and key lookup, while list membership is O(n), so use sets/dicts for fast lookups and deduplication.
Only hashable (immutable) objects can be dict keys or set elements, which is why tuples can serve as composite keys but lists cannot.
Dictionaries preserve insertion order (guaranteed since Python 3.7), while sets give no order guarantee, so never rely on set iteration order.
Comprehensions (and generator expressions for large data) are the idiomatic, efficient way to build and transform collections, and tuples/frozensets add safety through immutability.
